meta.title: Who really said "Freedom of the press is guaranteed only to those who own one"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not H. L. Mencken. A. J. Liebling wrote it in The New Yorker, 14 May 1960, in "Do You Belong in Journalism?" Quote Investigator confirms the credit.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Freedom of the press is guaranteed only to those who own one'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mencken — A. J. Liebling, in a parenthesis in The New Yorker of 14 May 1960. Mencken had been dead four years. Sources and chronology inside.

answer.label: Not H. L. Mencken — actually A. J. Liebling
answer.sourceLine: Liebling slipped the line into a parenthesis in his “Wayward Press” column “Do You Belong in Journalism?” in The New Yorker of 14 May 1960 (quote on page 109). Quote Investigator finds no support at all for the Mencken credit, and Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” on Mencken’s own page.

source.excerpt: (Freedom of the press is guaranteed only to those who own one.)
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ reports that an exact match to this wording was printed in The New Yorker in 1960, in A. J. Liebling’s essay “The Wayward Press: Do You Belong in Journalism?” (14 May 1960, start page 105, quotation page 109), and that the leading reference works — Fred R. Shapiro’s Yale Book of Quotations (2006) and Ralph Keyes’ The Quote Verifier (2006) — credit Liebling on the strength of that citation.
Wikiquote’s Liebling page ↗ carries the line among his quotes with the same citation, The New Yorker (May 14, 1960).

On the other side of the ledger, Wikiquote’s H. L. Mencken page ↗ places the sentence in its Misattributed section, crediting A. J. Liebling and “Do you belong in journalism?”, The New Yorker (14 May 1960), and noting the common paraphrase “Freedom of press is limited to those who own one.”

Quote Investigator also records the pre-history: Norman Woelfel in 1941 on a press “free for those who own and control it,” and the Australian politician Arthur Calwell in 1944 and 1945 — thematically close, but QI judges the phrasing neither as elegant nor as funny ↗.
source.excerptNote: The brackets are Liebling’s own. In the surrounding paragraph he argues that the most useful thing Congress could do for struggling newspapers would be to raise the capital-gains tax to the level of the income tax — because anyone who can afford the price of a paper is, by definition, a businessman. The aphorism is an aside inside that argument, not a heading or a peroration. Quote Investigator notes it is not clear why Liebling parenthesised the line, and that he may possibly have been repeating an existing adage.

It was first published in The New Yorker on 14 May 1960 — well after the 1931 cut-off — by the F-R Publishing Corporation; the magazine was acquired by Advance Publications in 1985 ↗ and is published by Condé Nast. Treat the sentence as an attributed short quotation from an in-copyright work rather than free-to-reuse text.

author.name: A. J. Liebling
author.heading: Who was A. J. Liebling?
author.metaLine: 1904–1963 · American journalist & New Yorker press critic
author.bio: Abbott Joseph Liebling was born in New York City on 18 October 1904 and was associated with The New Yorker from 1935 until his death on 28 December 1963. He wrote the magazine’s “Wayward Press” feature, a running critique of American newspapers, and is also the man who stuck Chicago with the nickname “the Second City.” Outside press criticism he is best remembered for The Sweet Science (1956), his collection of boxing essays.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and why that fails
misattribution.intro: This is a clean case of a good line drifting to a more famous curmudgeon. Liebling was a press critic; Mencken was the press curmudgeon. Over time the sentence migrated, and the wording frayed as it went.

items.why: Quote Investigator’s verdict is one sentence long: the linkage to H. L. Mencken is unsupported ↗. The earliest reassignment QI could find is a 2010 book, Macs in the Ministry, half a century after Liebling’s column. Mencken’s dates, per Wikiquote ↗, are 12 September 1880 – 29 January 1956: he died four years before the essay ran, and Wikiquote files the quotation in the Misattributed section of his own page.

items.scope: Wording — “limited to those who own one”
items.who: A. J. Liebling (right author, altered words)
items.why: The “limited” variant is the one usually attached to Mencken. Quote Investigator records it in Barbara Rowes’ 1979 The Book of Quotes credited to Liebling, and again in the 2010 Macs in the Ministry credited to Mencken; Wikiquote ↗ treats it as a paraphrase of the 1960 original.

items.scope: Wording — “belongs to the man who owns one” / “confined to the people who own one”
items.who: A. J. Liebling (right author, altered words)
items.why: Both are later rewrites. QI cites a 1976 column in The Lincoln Star for the “belongs to the man who owns one” form and James G. Bellows’ 2002 memoir The Last Editor for “confined to the people who own one” — both credited to Liebling, neither matching what he printed ↗.

Quote Investigator documents thematically similar remarks in the 1940s ↗ — Woelfel on a press “free for those who own and control it,” and Calwell in the Australian House of Representatives — but describes them as less elegant and compact, and without the humorous edge. They are not the quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact sentence is A. J. Liebling’s, printed parenthetically in The New Yorker of 14 May 1960; Quote Investigator credits him and rejects the Mencken attribution outright ↗.

context.heading: Why a parenthesis became the most quoted line in press criticism
lead: Liebling did not write it as an aphorism. He wrote it as an aside. The sentence sits inside round brackets in the middle of a paragraph about tax policy and newspaper economics — his argument being that a paper is a business first, and that whoever can afford the purchase price sets the limits of what gets printed. The joke lands because it is thrown away.

Quote Investigator flags an honest uncertainty about those brackets: it is not clear why Liebling parenthesised the line, and he may have been repeating something already in the air. Thematically similar remarks were circulating in the 1940s — the American educator Norman Woelfel in 1941, and the Australian politician Arthur Calwell in the House of Representatives in 1944 and 1945 — but none of them had Liebling’s compression or his humour, and none of them is the sentence people quote.
detailsBody: Eight years before Liebling’s column, the opposite sentiment was in print as newspaper filler. Quote Investigator records a boxed item on the front page of The Gettysburg Times of 2 May 1952 — and the same line as filler in The Daily Notes of Canonsburg, Pennsylvania, on 7 May 1952 — insisting that freedom of the press belongs to the people of a nation rather than to the owners of publications. Liebling’s version is the cynical answer to that idealistic one, and it is the version that survived.
